questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Third-Degree Taylor Polynomial For a Given Function About a Given Point
questions.problem: The third-degree Taylor polynomial of  ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the third-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we plug $a=\frac{\pi }{4}$ into the general formula to give

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =f(\frac{\pi }{4})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})\frac{1}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+{f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{4})\frac{1}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3} \\  & =f(\frac{\pi }{4})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}){(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+\frac{1}{6}{f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{4}){(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to compute $f(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ ${f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ and ${f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={cos}^{2}⁡x & ⟹ &  & f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=-1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug the results for $f(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ ${f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ and ${f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ into our third-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}-(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{0}{2}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+\frac{4}{6}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{2}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Third-Degree Taylor Polynomial For a Function Given Some Derivatives
questions.problem: Let $f$ be a function with $f(2)=3,{f}^{′}(2)=2,{f}^{″}(2)=-4$ and ${f}^{‴}(2)=6.$ Which of the following is the third-degree Taylor polynomial for $f$ about $x=2?$
questions.worked_solution:
The third-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =f(2)+{f}^{′}(2)(x-2)+\frac{{f}^{″}(2)}{2!}(x-2)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(2)}{3!}(x-2)^{3} \\  & =f(2)+{f}^{′}(2)(x-2)+\frac{{f}^{″}(2)}{2}(x-2)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(2)}{6}(x-2)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We have been given the following set of values: 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & =3 \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =2 \\ {f}^{″}(2) & =-4 \\ {f}^{‴}(2) & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given values into our Taylor polynomial, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =3+2(x-2)+\frac{-4}{2}(x-2)^{2}+\frac{6}{6}(x-2)^{3} \\  & =3+2(x-2)-2(x-2)^{2}+(x-2)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The third-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ about $x=0$ is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the third-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x+{f}^{″}(0)\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}+{f}^{‴}(0)\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!} \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x+{f}^{″}(0)\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{f}^{‴}(0)\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to compute $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ ${f}^{″}(0),$ and ${f}^{‴}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡0=0 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡0=-1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}(0) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡0=0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug the results for $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ ${f}^{″}(0),$ and ${f}^{‴}(0)$ into our third-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =1+0\cdot x-1\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+0\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{6} \\  & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Coefficient of a Term In the Third-Degree Taylor Polynomial of a Given Function
questions.problem: What is the coefficient of $(x-1)^{3}$ in the third-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$ about $x=1?$
questions.worked_solution:
The coefficient of $(x-1)^{3}$ is $\frac{1}{3!}{f}^{(3)}(1).$ Let's compute the necessary derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt[3]{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-2/3} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{2}{9}{x}^{-5/3} \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{10}{27}{x}^{-8/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate ${f}^{‴}(1),$ which gives

$$
{f}^{‴}(-1)=\frac{10}{27}\cdot {1}^{-8/3}=\frac{10}{27}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{3!}{f}^{‴}(1)=\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{10}{27}=\frac{5}{81}.
$$

So the coefficient of $(x-1)^{3}$ is $\frac{5}{81}.$

questions.problem:
Find the coefficient of ${(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}$ in the third-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ about $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Do not round the answer.

The coefficient of ${(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}$ is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The coefficient of ${(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}$ is $\frac{1}{3!}{f}^{‴}(-\frac{\pi }{2}).$ Let's compute the necessary derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate ${f}^{‴}(-\frac{\pi }{2}),$ which gives

$$
{f}^{‴}(-\frac{\pi }{2})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})=-1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{3!}{f}^{‴}(-\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{1}{6}\cdot (-1)=-\frac{1}{6}.
$$

So, the coefficient of ${(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}$ is $-\frac{1}{6}.$
